implementation_notes: In Go the budget travels inside the call signature rather than in a wrapper: context.WithTimeout derives a child Context whose Done channel closes when the budget expires, Deadline() exposes the absolute time, and Err() reports context.DeadlineExceeded; the convention that every blocking function takes ctx as its first parameter makes database/sql, net/http and gRPC honour the same budget without extra plumbing. The cancel function must be called (defer cancel()) or the timer survives until the parent context ends, and a derived context takes the sooner of its own timeout and the parent's deadline, so a call-level timeout composes with an inbound request budget. net.Dialer.Timeout and http.Client.Timeout remain the coarse per-client guards, not the call-level mechanism.
pitfalls: Every WithTimeout/WithCancel must have its cancel called: otherwise the timer and the child context stay alive until the parent is cancelled (go vet reports lostcancel).
Deriving from context.Background() inside a request drops the caller's budget; derive from the incoming context so the earlier deadline wins.
A timeout and an explicit cancel both arrive as a wrapped context error, so classify with errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) (or ctx.Err()) instead of matching error strings.
Cancellation is advisory: goroutines and the server-side handler keep running unless they select on ctx.Done(), so a timeout without propagation still burns work.
